The controls beside an annotated expression name that expression. A request
keeps its button in the keyboard order while it is being prepared; moving to
another control keeps your chosen position. Brief status messages announce when
a result is available. Read the transcript or authored braille text separately:
those results are not automatically spoken again and do not replace MathJax's
native accessible representation or establish that a proposed meaning is correct.

::: {#thm-positive-square name="Positive squares" semantic-id="https://example.org/maths/positive-square"}
For every non-zero real number $x$, the square $x^2$ is positive.
:::

See @thm-positive-square. [Open its proof](#prf-positive-square) or
[jump to the hint](#hint-sign).

:::: {#prf-positive-square .proof proof-for="#thm-positive-square" am-summary="Proof of positive squares"}
If $x>0$, the product $x\cdot x$ is positive. If $x<0$, then $-x>0$
and $x\cdot x=(-x)\cdot(-x)>0$.

::: {#hint-sign .am-hint theorem-for="#thm-positive-square" am-summary="Hint: consider both signs"}
Consider the positive and negative cases separately.
:::
::::

::: {#assumption-real .am-assumption theorem-for="#thm-positive-square"}
The statement concerns non-zero elements of the ordered field of real numbers.
:::

::: {#explanation-intro .am-explanation theorem-for="#thm-positive-square" am-summary="Intuitive explanation" am-level="Introductory"}
Two positive factors give a positive product. Two negative factors also give
a positive product. The non-zero condition excludes a square of zero.
:::

::: {#explanation-advanced .am-explanation theorem-for="#thm-positive-square" am-summary="Explanation using order axioms" am-level="Advanced"}
In the ordered field of real numbers, either $x>0$ or $-x>0$ when $x\ne0$.
The product of two positive elements is positive, and $(-x)^2=x^2$.
:::

::: {#def-ordered-pair name="Ordered pair" semantic-id="https://example.org/maths/ordered-pair" am-macro="amPair" am-args="first second" am-intent="ordered-pair($first,$second)" am-tex="(#1,#2)"}
The declared notation denotes an ordered pair with first and second components.
:::

The pair is $\amPair{a}{b}$. Numerical and structured examples are
$\amPair{1}{2}$ and $\amPair{x^2}{y+1}$.

These annotations record authored meaning. Their survival in MathML does not
establish speech interpretation, mathematical correctness or accessibility conformance.

## Try the optional transcript

Render this file to HTML, then use its intent transcript controls. Compare the
ordered pair above with the interval below: both display as $(a,b)$, while the
authored meanings differ. Requesting a transcript does not replace the native
mathematics or its accessible name. If MathJax speech is disabled or unavailable,
the control explains the fallback.

::: {#def-open-interval name="Open interval" semantic-id="https://example.org/maths/open-interval" am-macro="amInterval" am-args="lower upper" am-intent="open-interval($lower,$upper)" am-tex="(#1,#2)"}
For real $a<b$, this interval contains the real numbers strictly between them.
:::

The interval is $\amInterval{a}{b}$.

::: {#def-absolute-value name="Absolute value" semantic-id="https://example.org/maths/absolute-value" am-macro="amAbsolute" am-args="value" am-intent="absolute-value($value)" am-tex="|#1|"}
For a real number, this is its distance from zero.
:::

Try $\amAbsolute{x}$ and $\amPair{\amAbsolute{x}}{y}$. Review the resulting
English text; the finite templates are experimental. Read the README for
supported grammar, reader-setting behaviour and the separate presentation-based
braille request. Ordinary theorem writing in `example.qmd` needs none of these
experimental settings.

## Try nested meaning without changing the original mathematics

::: {#def-power name="Power" semantic-id="https://example.org/maths/power" am-macro="amPower" am-args="base exponent" am-intent="power($base,$exponent)" am-tex="#1^{#2}"}
The second argument is the exponent of the first argument.
:::

::: {#def-fraction name="Fraction" semantic-id="https://example.org/maths/fraction" am-macro="amFraction" am-args="numerator denominator" am-intent="fraction($numerator,$denominator)" am-tex="\\frac{#1}{#2}"}
The first argument is the numerator; the second is the denominator.
:::

Request a transcript for $\amFraction{\amPower{x}{2}}{\amAbsolute{y}}$.
The native expression remains a fraction with numerator $x^2$ and denominator
$|y|$. Compare the operand order and grouping in the optional transcript.
Its wording is experimental; the transcript does not establish that $y$ is
nonzero or that the expression is defined in a chosen mathematical context.
